guidance: A field reader, not a validator: the bytes are trusted and a header that parses is not necessarily well formed for its purpose. The checksum cannot verify when the paste ends at the header, because the sum covers the data too, and a NIC with checksum offload can leave a placeholder. A SYN segment's own window is never scaled, and the shift negotiated in a handshake is not visible in any later segment. This page makes no capture and reads no traffic.
method: The header is read at the offsets RFC 9293 Figure 1 gives it: a 16-bit source port, a 16-bit destination port, the 32-bit sequence number, the 32-bit acknowledgment number, then one byte whose high nibble is the data offset in 32-bit words and whose low nibble is the four reserved bits, one byte of control flags (CWR 0x80, ECE 0x40, URG 0x20, ACK 0x10, PSH 0x08, RST 0x04, SYN 0x02, FIN 0x01), the 16-bit window, the 16-bit checksum, the 16-bit urgent pointer and the options that fill the header out to four times the data offset. A data offset below five words, or one that reaches past the bytes pasted, is refused rather than padded. Options are walked in order: kinds 0 and 1 are one byte, every other option carries a length byte that counts its own two bytes, a length below two or one that leaves the header is refused, and the content after an end-of-list option must be zero padding. An MSS option is read as a 16-bit value, a window scale as its shift count (above the RFC 7323 cap of 14 it is reported as 14), a SACK option as 64-bit block pairs of left and right edges, and a timestamps option as TSval and TSecr; other kinds are named from the IANA TCP Option Kind Numbers registry and shown as hex. The checksum is the 16-bit one's complement of the one's complement sum of a pseudo-header and the whole segment with the checksum field zeroed. The IPv4 pseudo-header is the two addresses, a zero byte, protocol 6 and the segment length; the IPv6 pseudo-header is both 128-bit addresses, a 32-bit upper-layer length, three zero bytes and 6 (RFC 8200 section 8.1). Because the sum covers the data, a segment pasted as its header alone will not verify, and a segment copied off a NIC that leaves checksum offload on can carry a placeholder instead of a real value. A window advertised in a segment with the SYN bit set is never scaled, so the window scale from the handshake is only applied to the other segments and is taken from the pseudo-header-adjacent field the user supplies. The window field is read unsigned. Payload bytes past the header are counted and shown as hex but not interpreted, port names are not looked up, and a segment is not reassembled or validated against a connection state.
